messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 50-year-old plumber who had built much of his identity around being the man other people called when something was broken. He had immigrated to the United States years earlier from West Africa, married, and settled into a life organized around early job calls, heavy tool bags, crawl spaces, and the steady confidence that he could handle himself. That changed after an assault several months ago. He had been finishing a late repair at a small commercial property and was loading equipment into his van when a man came up quickly from the side of the building, demanded money, and struck him when he hesitated. What stays with Kwame is not a clean story but flashes: the sudden movement at the edge of his vision, the man’s arm lifting, the glint of metal from a tool lying near his own open van, the pavement rushing up, and the feeling that in the crucial second he did nothing right. When he tries to describe it, his words thin out. He says he can “see it all” but cannot tell it straight through, and each return of those images brings a crushing sense that he failed some basic test of judgment and strength.

In the first weeks afterward, Kwame found himself replaying those pictures without warning. He did not think of them as memories arriving in an orderly way; they were more like abrupt visual intrusions that took over his attention. A figure stepping out from behind shelving at the hardware store, a customer appearing beside him while he worked under a sink, even his wife moving suddenly in the kitchen could pull his body into the same jolt of danger before he had time to think. At night he lay awake braced for something he could not name, and when he did sleep it was shallow and easily broken. The more these picture-like fragments returned, the more certain he became that danger was close and that his body had to stay ready.

As the months passed, the meaning Kwame made of the assault hardened. He had come to believe that what happened was profoundly unfair and that no one had answered for it, and that belief kept the event feeling unfinished rather than over. Even more painful was the conclusion he drew about himself. Before, he had thought of himself as capable, decisive, the person who knew what to do in tight spaces and difficult situations. Now he was certain he could not trust himself to respond correctly if something happened again. That loss of confidence narrowed his world. He only felt truly safe in a very limited set of places—his bedroom with the door locked, a particular chair in his living room, his own truck when parked in his driveway—and outside those places he scanned constantly. On jobs, if someone moved unexpectedly in a hallway or came up behind him while he was checking pipes, he would jerk, turn sharply, and feel ashamed immediately afterward. In his mind, the problem was not only that the world had become dangerous, but that he was no longer the man who could manage it.

That sense of threat fed back into the way the assault lived in his mind. Because he spent so much of each day on edge, sleeping lightly and startling at sudden movement, the event never settled into the past. Instead, it kept returning in fragments, vivid and sensory, especially when he was tired. He might be crouched under a sink in a client’s bathroom, hear footsteps entering the room, and in an instant be back inside the same visual burst of the attack, unable to put any of it into words except to say, “I see it.” The guilt arrived with the images: he should have noticed sooner, moved faster, protected himself better. His wife has seen him sit silent after one of these episodes, staring ahead, unable to explain what just passed through him.

The assault has altered his work and his marriage in concrete ways. He now avoids late service calls whenever he can and refuses jobs in isolated buildings, which has begun to affect his income and has led to tension with a contractor who used to rely on him. Even routine appointments are difficult because plumbing work places him exactly where he feels most exposed—bent over, focused on a task, with people entering and leaving around him. At home, he keeps to his few safe places and checks locks repeatedly before bed. The nights are the worst; once awake, he listens for movement and cannot relax enough to return to sleep.

Kwame finally sought help after startling so violently when a customer came around a corner at a job that he dropped a wrench and cut his hand. What frightened him most was not the injury but the thought, immediate and familiar, that he could no longer trust himself to do the right thing in a critical moment. He says he wants to sleep, to work without feeling hunted, and to be able to tell what happened without being overtaken by the pictures and the guilt. At the same time, he is afraid that the assault revealed something permanent—that his world is no longer safe except in a few shrinking places, and that the capable man he was before may not return.
